### Problem: Two Sum {#sec-hash-p1-a}

::: {.p-statement}
Given an array $a$ of $n$ integers ($2 \le n \le 10^4$, $-10^9 \le a_i, t \le 10^9$) and a target $t$, return the **indices** of the two elements that sum to $t$. Exactly one valid pair exists, and you may not use the same element twice. Return the pair as $(i, j)$ with $i < j$.

Source: [LC 1 · Two Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
You are not searching for "any pair summing to $t$" — for each $x$ there is exactly **one value** that could partner with it, namely $t - x$. One value means one lookup, and a lookup means the problem is $O(n)$ once you own a "what have I seen, and where" table.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Brute force.** Every pair $(i, j)$ with $i < j$: $O(n^2)$ checks — up to $5\cdot10^7$ at $n = 10^4$, over budget in Python.
2. **Index the whole array first.** Build `pos = {value: index}`, then for each $i$ look up $t - a_i$ and reject the hit when it *is* $i$. $O(n)$, but two passes and one explicit self-pair check.
3. **Query the seen map, then join it.** One pass: at $i$, `seen` holds only indices $< i$, so a hit is automatically a valid partner — the `j != i` test disappears because the invariant forbids it (@sec-hash-complement).

**Invariant.** Before the query at position $i$, `seen` maps exactly the values of $[0, i)$ to their indices.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Check every pair

::: {.form-next}
The definition, verbatim: try all $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs and return the first that adds to $t$. Correct and provably so — and $O(n^2)$, which at $n = 10^4$ is around fifty million comparisons in Python.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def two_sum_brute(a, t):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if a[i] + a[j] == t:
                return (i, j)
    return None
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> twoSumBrute(vector<int>& a, int t) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j)
            if ((long long)a[i] + a[j] == t)   // up to 2e9: keep a margin with long long
                return {i, j};
    return {};
}
```
:::

#### Index the whole array first

::: {.form-next}
Replace "search the array for $t - a_i$" with "one lookup in a value-to-index map" — but the map must be built before any query, so it contains $a_i$ itself. $O(n)$ now, at the price of a second pass and an explicit `j != i` guard.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def two_sum_two_pass(a, t):
    pos = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        pos[x] = i
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        j = pos.get(t - x)
        if j is not None and j != i:
            return (i, j) if i < j else (j, i)
    return None
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
using namespace std;

vector<int> twoSumTwoPass(vector<int>& a, int t) {
    unordered_map<long long, int> pos;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) pos[a[i]] = i;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) {
        auto it = pos.find((long long)t - a[i]);
        if (it != pos.end() && it->second != i)
            return {min(i, it->second), max(i, it->second)};
    }
    return {};
}
```
:::

#### Query the seen map, then join it

::: {.form-next}
Move the insert *after* the query and merge the passes into one. Now `seen` only ever summarises indices strictly below $i$, so every hit is a genuine partner — the self-pair bug is not "handled", it is unrepresentable. This is the order discipline of @sec-hash-complement in its purest form.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("twosum", "seen")
    assert str(final) == "(0, 1)"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-two-sum
def two_sum(a: list[int], t: int) -> tuple[int, int] | None:
    seen = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        j = seen.get(t - x)
        if j is not None:
            return (j, i)
        seen[x] = i
    return None


def all_pairs(a, t):
    return [(i, j) for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a))
            if a[i] + a[j] == t]


checked = 0
for _ in range(1500):
    a = [random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 9))]
    t = random.randint(-18, 18)
    got = two_sum(a, t)
    pairs = all_pairs(a, t)
    if not pairs:
        assert got is None and two_sum_brute(a, t) is None
        assert two_sum_two_pass(a, t) is None
    else:
        assert got in pairs and two_sum_brute(a, t) == pairs[0]
        assert two_sum_two_pass(a, t) in pairs
        checked += 1
assert checked > 300                     # the unique-solution regime is covered
assert two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == (0, 1)    # the board sample
assert two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6) == (1, 2)
assert two_sum([3, 3], 6) == (0, 1)            # t = 2x: query-first is what saves you
print("two_sum OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
using namespace std;

vector<int> twoSum(vector<int>& a, int t) {
    unordered_map<long long, int> seen;    // value -> index, only indices < i
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) {
        auto it = seen.find((long long)t - a[i]);   // find() never inserts; long long: margin
        if (it != seen.end()) return {it->second, i};
        seen[a[i]] = i;                    // ... and only now join the range
    }
    return {};
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Check every pair** is $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Index the whole array first** is $O(n)$ expected time and $O(n)$ space, with two passes. **Query the seen map, then join it** is $O(n)$ expected time and $O(n)$ space in one pass, and stops you from ever writing the self-pair bug; on `unordered_map` with `int` keys, remember @sec-hash-anti if the input is adversarial.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $t = 2x$ with two copies of $x$: the answer is the pair of copies. Query-first finds it; insert-first would pair the first copy with itself.
- A single element with $a_i = t/2$ is not a solution: the two indices must differ, and query-first never reports $(i, i)$.
- Negatives: the complement $t - x$ can lie outside the range of the values; a hash map does not care, a frequency array would need an offset (@sec-arr-p5).
- Overflow in C++: with $|a_i|, |t| \le 10^9$, both $a_i + a_j$ and $t - a_i$ can reach $\pm 2\cdot10^9$. That still fits in a 32-bit `int` (limit about $2.147\cdot10^9$), but only just; the listings compute in `long long` so that a variant with slightly larger values cannot overflow (@sec-arr-cost).
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CSES 1640 · Sum of Two Values](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1640) — the same problem with 1-based positions and $n$ up to $2\cdot10^5$; print `IMPOSSIBLE` when no pair exists.
- [CF 1931D · Divisible Pairs](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1931/D){rating="1300"} — the complement of $a_i$ is a pair of remainders, $(-a_i \bmod x,\ a_i \bmod y)$, looked up before inserting.
:::
